Author: @hwertz10
Content:
So the reason the Steam machines really failed was (at the time) Linux.  I say this as a Linux user since 1993.   Linux desktops were great by 2016, but the 3D drivers weren't; and wine was like 95% feature complete, but lots of software used that other 5%.  These two aspects are a night-and-day difference then compared to in the 2020s.

Mesa Gallium 3D drivers only came out within the last 5 or 6 years, which are WAAAY better than the previous 3D drivers (for Intel and AMD/ATI hardware... Nvidia has had excellent drivers all along.).  

Wine (and dxvk, vkd3d... and so Steam Proton) were not in the shape they are now.   If they'd had the current-day software stack back then, these boxes would have probably been quite successuful (literally, Mesa Gallium supports GPUs going back about 20 years, so the present-day modern drivers would support whatever was in these decks in 2016.)  Compatibility now is "100% unless the game has anti-cheat that specifically excludes Linux/Wine/Proton."  Having games not run is VERY uncommon rather than (as you say) the 20% compatibility back then.

Author: @PustulioYo-s9s
Content:
Sega is the company responsible for delaying the Sonic movie, let's give credit where credit is due. 
Paramount is simply a distributor in this situation, they have almost no creative control over the final product when it comes to the Sonic the Hedgehog film series. 
For all intents and purposes, the films are 100% made by Sega, they are the main production company, they own and control the IP rights, they personally provided all the character designs and animation, hell, even the director cut his teeth directing cutscenes for older Sega games like Shadow the Hedgehog. 
The only things Paramount had direct control over were the amount of advertising and the actual stars of the film, it would not surprise me if they are the reason the likes of Idris Elba, Jim Carrey, Keanu Reeves, and Ben Schwartz are in the series, but these films would have been made whether Paramount picked up the series or not, they just would have been released under a different distributor.
So, yeah, there's no thanking Paramount here, in fact, they were probably the ones who pushed for his original design, after all, they were the ones putting their reputation on the line by releasing the original trailer, the Sonic series reputation was already tarnished at that point, we were all expecting it to be bad and the internet was ready and willing to laugh at the trailer. 
The only reason the end product ended up being so good is because it's a Hollywood movie based on a video game...... that's made by a video game developer, Hollywood still does not understand how to make a video game adaptation and the two times where I feel like it is worked, the Sonic series and Detective Pikachu, is because the developers were directly involved themselves, making sure everything was going in the direction they wanted.

Author: @Dinchev666
Content: Soooo, regarding a service like Incogni. All similar brokers have an option to "plead" for them to remove the data. Hell for Europeans under GDPR they are mandatory to remove it upon request. If they use it after a request has been pushed, you can sue them. So all this platform does is push those requests from one place. Yes it grants visibility and makes easy for you to send requests to data brokers, but there is no real guarantee that hey will accept it. Also, most scams come from leaked data, not brokers. So better, check if your phone for exampel has been leaked when you receive such Smishing. You can do it in Haveibeenpwned and it will show you. In most cases that will be the cause. Just saying so that you know what to expect.

Author: @Jdbye
Content: Ultimately, Steam Machines were not a failure. They were what led to the Steam Deck, which has been a huge success. If Valve didn't create Steam Big Picture mode and SteamOS to go with the Steam Machines, the Steam Deck would not exist or it would be very different experience, running Windows like most other gaming handheld PCs on the market, which would'be an inferior experience. And the Steam Controller DNA which remains in the Steam Deck plays a significant role in making certain types of games more accessible without mouse and keyboard. Handheld gaming PCs existed before the Steam Deck, from companies like GPD, but it's safe to say that the Steam Deck revolutionized the gaming handheld market and Steam Machines deserve credit for leading Valve down the road that eventually led to that.

Just a note about the last item of who has your personal details.

Every time you sign your name to something it is at risk of being recorded & on sold to a data list. That includes loyalty cards (you didn't think they were interested in you saving $1, did you?), open homes, websites etc etc.

This is what scammers use to call you up and open with "Hi I'm from Microsoft and you have a virus on your PC..." Usually they use an auto dialer and as soon as you answer they connect you to an agent which is why there's a delay before they speak to you. Altho I note that they've started using automated recordings where you have to push a digit to be connected.... Probably didn't like my referees whistle in their ear.

Author: @macnkeebs
Content:
i don't necessarily consider it misinformation given the overarching story behind honey, and it's honestly a drop in the bucket in consideration of the rest, but @25:33 - is something that was a bit misleading from the original vid. what honey is guaranteeing the businesses that they give them the ability to dictate what coupon codes are allowed, along with exclusive ones for honey users only. there are other sites that will make profit from affiliate-offered coupons/codes, which won't be tracked back to the user themselves, but to the coupon site itself. some businesses, depending on just how massive they are, won't necessarily kill old or outdated coupon codes, which leads to things like that "welcome15" submitted code being something that might be meant specifically for new customers who sign up for email marketing, not being tracked to those specific efforts.

it's why the whole "we'll share once our system reviews it" likely pops up. it could cross check with codes that the business is saying "no, don't allow these to be used because this is how we track our newsletter or promotional budget" or "no, this is meant specifically for youtuberxyz and won't get tracked back to them correctly". do things still slip through? probably. again, depending on the business size and who is specifically at the helm of tracking these things, it isn't always the case. sometimes, they might even be okay with an old code still working as it could match or be less than more legitimate ones that they offer through their own media or affiliates, but it's to protect not only the business from losing money, but from consumers unknowingly using a code that won't get tracked to the actual affiliate that it was created for.

i know some will say "well boohoo, i want the best deal available no matter where it comes from!" --- but i'm sure there are sites or advertisers that you don't want to be associated with, yet are using codes meant for them. yeah, they lose out on making any money, but you're still using something that was created for their benefit. on the opposite side, you could unwillingly use a code that should go to someone you really do care for and would support, yet they'll never know of it and the business won't be able to support better fees for that creator.

There is a reason Valve decided to make the Steam Deck themselves.

6. Overwatch 2 Launch - Faced server issues, player dissatisfaction, and missing promised features, leading to a significant drop in player engagement.


7. Spotify’s Car Thing - An unnecessary device for controlling Spotify, which led to a class-action lawsuit after the company discontinued support.


8. Sonos App Redesign - The redesign removed essential features, causing a revenue drop and the resignation of the CEO.
